title: Symposium
author: Plato
openingText: As for what you're asking about, I believe I'm well prepared to answer. In fact, the day before yesterday I was on my way into the city from my home in Phalerum when an acquaintance of mine caught sight of me from behind and called out playfully from a distance, 'Apollodorus! You there — you Phalerian! Halt!' (Source note: Probably a pun on a Greek word meaning 'bald-headed'.) So I did as I was told, and he said, 'Apollodorus, I was just looking for you. I wanted to ask you about the speeches in praise of love that Socrates, Alcibiades, and others gave at Agathon's supper. Someone told me what he had heard from Phoenix, the son of Philip, but his account was very vague. He did say, though, that you knew about them, so I'd like to hear them from you. Who better than you to report your friend's words? But first tell me,' he said, 'were you at that gathering yourself?'
about:
At a dinner celebrating Agathon's victory as a tragic playwright, the guests agree to take turns praising Eros, the god of love. Their speeches offer different accounts of desire: as a source of courage, a distinction between kinds of attachment, a harmony of opposites, or a search for a missing half. Socrates questions Agathon and recounts what Diotima taught him about love, creation and beauty.

The arrival of the drunken Alcibiades changes the gathering. His account of loving Socrates brings the discussion back to the difficulties of an individual relationship. Apollodorus narrates the evening from Aristodemus's recollection, so the book also asks us to listen to stories told through other people. The speeches reflect ancient social roles and assumptions; the speakers disagree, and their claims invite comparison.

angleCards.title: Compare the accounts of love
angleCards.text: Each speaker gives love a different purpose. Track what each account explains, what it leaves out, and how later speakers respond.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to compare the competing accounts of love and judge the arguments rather than assume they all express the same view.

angleCards.title: Follow Diotima's argument
angleCards.text: Diotima moves from desire for what we lack to creation, immortality and beauty itself. Follow each step and consider whether it follows from the last.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to understand and test the steps in Diotima's account, including the ascent from one beautiful body to beauty itself.

angleCards.title: Alcibiades and the difficulty of change
angleCards.text: Alcibiades says Socrates makes him recognize his failings, yet he still seeks public approval. Compare understanding what to do with actually doing it.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to explore what Alcibiades's story reveals about desire, self-knowledge and changing one's life.

angleCards.title: The missing half
angleCards.text: Aristophanes imagines humans split in two and searching for reunion. Later, Diotima questions whether people want their own half or what is good. Examine that disagreement.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to compare Aristophanes's myth of reunion with Diotima's argument about the good.

cast.name: Socrates
cast.description: Arrives late after stopping to think. He questions Agathon and recounts Diotima's teaching. Alcibiades later makes him the subject of a very personal speech.

cast.name: Alcibiades
cast.description: Enters drunk and asks to join the drinking. His speech praises Socrates while also complaining about the philosopher's resistance to his advances.

cast.name: Aristophanes
cast.description: Hiccups make him exchange speaking turns with Eryximachus. His story imagines round, double humans whom Zeus divides, leaving each half longing for reunion.

cast.name: Diotima
cast.description: A woman from Mantineia whose teaching Socrates reports. She questions his assumptions about love and describes a path from particular beauties toward beauty itself.

cast.name: Agathon
cast.description: A tragic playwright celebrating a victory. His elaborate praise of Eros prompts Socrates to ask whether love possesses the beauty and goodness it desires.

cast.name: Phaedrus
cast.description: His complaint that Eros deserves more praise inspires the evening's proposal. He speaks first, linking love with courage and the desire to act honorably.

whyItMatters.title: A conversation with competing voices
whyItMatters.body: The speeches differ in method as well as conclusion: myth, poetic praise, medical analogy and questioning each play a part. Reading them together makes the differences between a moving story and a convincing argument worth examining.

whyItMatters.title: Love and the search for wholeness
whyItMatters.body: Aristophanes gives longing the shape of a search for a missing half. Diotima then asks whether reunion is desirable unless it is also good. The contrast opens a question about what we seek in another person.

whyItMatters.title: From attraction to understanding
whyItMatters.body: Diotima's ascent connects attraction to bodies with appreciation of souls, laws and knowledge. It culminates in beauty itself. Alcibiades's following speech invites the reader to compare that ideal with a difficult personal attachment.
